after.worked_solution:
A Riccati differential equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x).
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$, we have

$$
y=z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x=(z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,(z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =({z}^{2}+2z\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,z-2{cos}^{2}⁡x+({cos}^{2}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ {z}^{′}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={z}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This is a Bernoulli equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x){z}^{n}
$$

where

$$
P(x)=0,\,Q(x)=1,\,n=2.
$$

A Riccati differential equation has the form

y′=a(x)y2+b(x)y+c(x).

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution y(x)=z(x)+y0(x), where y0(x) is a known particular solution. Differentiating gives y′(x)=z′(x)+y0′(x).

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation: z′−sin⁡x=(z+cos⁡x)2−2cos⁡x(z+cos⁡x)+(cos2⁡x−sin⁡x).

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify: z′−sin⁡x=(z2+2zcos⁡x+cos2⁡x)−2cos⁡xz−2cos2⁡x+(cos2⁡x−sin⁡x)z′−sin⁡x=z2−sin⁡xz′=z2

after.worked_solution:
The equation

$$
{y}^{′}=4{y}^{2}-8{e}^{x}y+4{e}^{2x}+{e}^{x},
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=4,\,b(x)=-8{e}^{x},\,c(x)=4{e}^{2x}+{e}^{x}.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)={e}^{x}.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)={e}^{x}$, we have

$$
y=z+{e}^{x}\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+{e}^{x}.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$

after.worked_solution:
The equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-x\,{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y+1-{x}^{3},
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=-x,\,b(x)=2{x}^{2},\,c(x)=1-{x}^{3}.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=1$, we have

$$
y=z+x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+1.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}+1=-x\,(z+x)^{2}+2{x}^{2}(z+x)+1-{x}^{3}.
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}+1 & =-x({z}^{2}+2xz+{x}^{2})+2{x}^{2}z+2{x}^{3}+1-{x}^{3} \\ {z}^{′}+1 & =-x{z}^{2}+1 \\ {z}^{′} & =-x{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-x{z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-x \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int -x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int -x\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ z & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute $z=y-x$ to recover the initial variable $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C} \\ y-x & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C} \\ y & =x+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C}\end{aligned}

content.problem:
Given that ${y}_{0}(x)=x$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-x\,{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y+1-{x}^{3}
$$

find the general solution of the equation.
content.worked_solution:
The equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-x\,{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y+1-{x}^{3},
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=-x,\,b(x)=2{x}^{2},\,c(x)=1-{x}^{3}.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=1$, we have

$$
y=z+x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+1.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}+1=-x\,(z+x)^{2}+2{x}^{2}(z+x)+1-{x}^{3}.
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}+1 & =-x({z}^{2}+2xz+{x}^{2})+2{x}^{2}z+2{x}^{3}+1-{x}^{3} \\ {z}^{′}+1 & =-x{z}^{2}+1 \\ {z}^{′} & =-x{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-x{z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-x \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int -x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int -x\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ z & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute $z=y-x$ to recover the initial variable $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C} \\ y-x & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C} \\ y & =x+\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+C}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Given that y0(x)=sin⁡x is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

y′=y2−2sin⁡xy+sin2⁡x+cos⁡x

find the general solution of the equation.

a
y=sin⁡x+2x+C
b
y=sin⁡x+2x−C
c
y=sin⁡x−1x+C
d
y=sin⁡x+1x+C
e
y=sin⁡x−12x+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Set y=sin(x)+z. Substitution gives z'=z². Integrating yields −1/z=x+C, so y=sin(x)−1/(x+C), choice c. The particular solution y=sin(x) also remains a solution.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Given that ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

find the general solution of the equation.
after.worked_solution:
The equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x,
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=1,\,b(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,c(x)={sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we have

$$
y=z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =({sin}^{2}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+{z}^{2})-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+2{sin}^{2}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ={z}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =x+C \\ z & =-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute $z=y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ to recover the initial variable $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x+C}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

y′=y2−2sin⁡xy+sin2⁡x+cos⁡x

find the general solution of the equation.

a
y=sin⁡x+2x+C
b
y=sin⁡x+2x−C
c
y=sin⁡x−1x+C
d
y=sin⁡x+1x+C
e
y=sin⁡x−12x+C

EXPLANATION

The equation y′=y2−2sin⁡xy+sin2⁡x+cos⁡x, is a Riccati differential equation of the form y′=a(x)y2+b(x)y+c(x), where a(x)=1,b(x)=−2sin⁡x,c(x)=sin2⁡x+cos⁡x.

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution y(x)=z(x)+y0(x), where y0(x) is a known particular solution. Differentiating gives y′(x)=z′(x)+y0′(x).

In our case, y0(x)=sin⁡x. Since y0′(x)=cos⁡x, we have y=z+sin⁡x⇒y′=z′+cos⁡x.

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation: z′+cos⁡x=(z+sin⁡x)2−2sin⁡x(z+sin⁡x)+sin2⁡x+cos⁡x

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify: z′+cos⁡x=(sin2⁡x+2sin⁡xz+z2)−(2sin⁡xz+2sin2⁡x)+sin2⁡x+cos⁡xz′+cos⁡x=z2+cos⁡xz′=z2

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables: dzdx=z21z2dzdx=1∫1z2dzdxdx=∫dx∫z−2dz=∫dx−1z=x+Cz=−1x+C

where C is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute z=y−sin⁡x to recover the initial variable y:

z=−1x+Cy−sin⁡x=−1x+Cy=−1x+C+sin⁡x=sin⁡x−1x+C

Given that ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is a particular solution of the Riccati differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

find the general solution of the equation.
content.worked_solution:
The equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,y+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x,
$$

is a Riccati differential equation of the form

$$
{y}^{′}=a(x){y}^{2}+b(x)y+c(x),
$$

where

$$
a(x)=1,\,b(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,c(x)={sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

To reduce the given Riccati equation to a Bernoulli equation, we use the substitution

$$
y(x)=z(x)+{y}_{0}(x),
$$

where ${y}_{0}(x)$ is a known particular solution.
Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)={z}^{′}(x)+{y}_{0}^{′}(x).
$$

In our case, ${y}_{0}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Since ${y}_{0}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we have

$$
y=z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⇒\,{y}^{′}={z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Let's substitute these expressions into our Riccati equation:

$$
{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(z+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Now, we expand the right-hand side, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =({sin}^{2}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+{z}^{2})-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,z+2{sin}^{2}⁡x)+{sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ={z}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {z}^{′} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve the obtained equation using separation of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int {z}^{-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{z} & =x+C \\ z & =-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Finally, let's substitute $z=y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ to recover the initial variable $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\frac{1}{x+C} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x+C}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{1}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$
